entries.title: 20 Best Gifts for Men, Manly Men, and Manly Man Men (2026)
entries.summary: When you need something that’s as mannishly masculinized as you can get for the Man™ in your life, we have you covered.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

There are gifts for men. And then there are manly men gifts. Countless gift guides for the men in your life offer up the same neckties and tool sets and tasteful leather belts. And don't get us wrong: We're classy people, too. We like only the finest T-shirt a Savile Row tailor recommends, and anything themed for whiskey.

But this is a guide to the manliest gifts made for man men, menly objects ranging from the most classic of man totems to the most ridiculously hypermasculinized. Welcome to the red-hot tropics of the manosphere. Mere regular soap will not do when soap with the word “men” on it also exists. No mere shaving for us, when shaving can be aggressive. Enjoy.

For more men-themed gifts for man-themed men, check out our Gifts for Outdoorsy People, our Gifts for Dads Who Don't Need Anything, and Gifts for Golfers.

Updated October 2026: We've added a toiletry bag from SPC/LST, a pressure washer, a head shaver, and a giant flashlight; removed a couple sold-out options; and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

  • A Cannon for Pepper

    Männkitchen

    Pepper Cannon

    Shaking isn't manly. Grinding is manly. Cannons are manly. Grinding so dominantly that your pepper grinder can plausibly be called a cannon is manly. So is deftly tooled precision of any kind. But Männkitchen’s Pepper Cannon isn't an expensive gimmick for the insecure. Its stainless steel burrs will grind peppercorns to the exact right size, among 50 settings, and this will end up mattering to anybody who spends a lot of time seasoning meat or building a rub. The all-metal construction will last decades. And it'll grind your pepper so fast it'll feel like the Dust Bowl got spicy.

  • Bourdain’s Favorite Knife

    Global

    8-Inch Classic Chef’s Knife

    Every man needs a good knife. Probably two. One for his pocket. One for the kitchen. If you're going to get a good knife, why not Anthony Bourdain's? Maybe it's me, but I pretty much don't know a dude who doesn't have a tattered copy of Kitchen Confidential somewhere in his house. This Global 8-inch chef's knife is Bourdain's knife, the one he recommended to starting chefs. The one he recommended as a baseline good chef's knife for those at home. It is Japanese-made stainless steel, ice-hardened, lightweight. Seamless from its handle to its convex edge. The Global chef knife is economy itself. It is a knife that most chefs own eventually. Maybe the man in your life would also do with a good knife.

  • Lasers for Measuring Everything

    Mileseey

    S50 Green-Laser Distance Measure

    You know what men like? Knowing how long something is, or how far away it is. Know what they (I) don't like? Stretching out a dinky tape measure that keeps shimmying or bending or snapping back into the roll. The solution to everything is always lasers. Lasers can do anything. Just ask Elon Musk.

    Anyway, just point this Mileseey S50 at anything, press the button, set your starting measuring point, and it'll tell you how far away it is. (It measures to 1/32 of an inch, but I wouldn't trust it past 1/16 of an inch.) Get a tripod for it and you can also do point-to-point measurements from a distance. I've measured windows for fittings. Door jambs. Most of the rooms and spaces in my house. I've barely used tape for four months. Why use tape when you can use lasers? Mileseey says the green laser light on this S50 is more visible than red light during the daytime. Maybe this is true. There are also a whole lot of trigonometric functions I haven't figured out, and the included instructions are only half helpful. But mostly I just want to know: How big is that thing? How far away?

  • A Tactical Toiletry Bag

    SPC/LST

    System Kit

    A Real Man (™) is always mission-ready, whether he’s rappelling off a cliff or heading into the hotel bathroom to brush his teeth. That’s why he needs a multipurpose pouch made of water-resistant 600D Cordura Re/Cor. The military-inspired System Kit from SPC/LST features two sections that can snap together (one zips flat and has three internal pockets, while the other zips only on the top and has just one zippered pocket), along with a 20-mm side strap with a clip in case you need to attach it to your pack, truck, or parachute. —Kat Merck

  • The Manliest Grill Gloves

    Big Green Egg

    Hell Hands

    Nothing is manlier than overkill. Lots of grill gloves can take a little heat, and save you from a hospital visit on a grill day. But can they take you to the gates of hell? These Hell Hands grill gloves from Big Green Egg are rated up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They're made with thick cowhide that goes most of the way up to your elbows—and look like something you'd wear for the zombie apocalypse. The pads are made with thick, puncture-resistant Armortex fabric and stitched with Kevlar.

    I don't know if this makes these gloves bulletproof. But what I do know is that I have placed my palm flat onto a scalding 500-degree cast-iron pan while wearing one of these Hell Hands. I barely felt warmth, let alone heat. These gloves are monsters. But note that these gloves are thick enough that your hands will feel more like mittens than hands. You'll need to use manly finger strength to flex them.

  • The Most Tactical Pants

    Ten Thousand

    Tactical Pant

    These pants are the most tactical pants of all pants, according to WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson. Cargo pants look like a baggy bouquet of pockets. But these pants? They are for men of action. They are stretch canvas, svelte, sturdy. They have pockets inside other pockets, pockets that remove traces of being pockets. If you're the sort of guy who wants to look good, without looking like you want to look good, these pants are your pants.

  • An “Ultra-Tough” Cooler

    RTIC

    45QT Ultra-Tough Cooler

    You might wonder whether black is the most natural color for a cooler, given its propensity for absorbing heat. OK, and? Suck it up, and embrace the steely, Vader-esque manliness of this Ultra-Tough cooler from RTIC. It's roto-molded, natch, but it's also filled with 2.8 inches of foam. I have tested the 45-quart version while tailgating in temps where the cooler was actually helping keep our seltzers from exploding.

    The Ultra-Tough is a beast to carry by yourself (the manly way, the way John Wayne would carry a cooler) because it weighs almost 30 pounds empty. This means it's about 55 pounds with a 24-pack of Bud Light, and 60 pounds if you toss in a 5-pound bag of ice from the store. But the foam handles mounted on free-swinging ropes make it manageable. In terms of build quality, this RTIC cooler is actually a little more solid than the Yeti size 65 that I previously owned, especially when it comes to the leak-free screw-in drain plug. —Martin Cizmar

  • Beef in a Box

    Pat LaFrieda Meat Purveyors

    Delivery Steaks

    Pat LaFrieda is a New York butcher. His dad was a butcher, and his dad's dad was a butcher, and so was the dad before that. The first butcher became a butcher after he got in a fistfight outside a butcher shop. This is Naples, Italy, we're talking about, where you sell meat or you are the meat. (We made this proverb up, but it seems right.) Anyway, this is not just good but actually great beef in a box. Pat LaFrieda beef is the beef served at some of the most famous restaurants in New York. It will also come in the mail, wherever you are: fresh, never frozen. And then it goes on the fire. According to WIRED meat delivery guide boss Scott Gilbertson, smart people wait for that super-fresh beef with a catcher's mitt, then cook it right up. Beef this good, you don't make it wait.

  • The Manliest Jacket

    Flint and Tinder

    Lined Waxed Trucker Jacket

    Waxed canvas is a manly fabric. A working man's fabric. It sheds water like a senator sheds consequences. But unlike politicians, this jacket builds character over time. It becomes itself. It'll build your character, too—or at least make you into one. After all, this is the jacket Pedro Pascal wore in The Last of Us, worn and rubbed down until it became shades darker. Because this is what silent, manly men wear, and wardrobe people know this. And sure, this Flint and Tinder trucker's jacket doesn't breathe quite as well as boring, unwaxed cotton. It resists everything except compliments.

  • A T-Shirt for the Strong and Stout

    True Classic

    Crew Neck T-Shirt

    An American man gathers bulk over time. It is the burden he carries, like the weight of responsibility or the consequence of bacon. Anyway, this shirt is made for the stout at heart (and maybe middle) but strong of arm. It hugs the biceps and chest, showing off raw power. But unlike a lot of T-shirts, it doesn't blouse out like a 1950s nightshirt. It's a man's shirt. For men who are a lot of man. A reliable white T-shirt, and a black T-shirt, are needed by pretty much all men.

  • For Super Soft Brillo Beards

    Duke Cannon Supply Co.

    Best Damn Beard Oil

    If you put words Amazon doesn’t like in a product’s name, that immediately makes it more manly. To wit, there’s Duke Cannon’s Best Damn Beard Oil, for scratchy facial hair. This beard oil helps prevent ingrown hairs and makes facial hair feel softer to the touch. Though, please note, the bottle says explicitly that it’s “not for clowns,” so don’t buy this for any Pagliaccis in your life. —Eric Ravenscraft

  • For Powerful Coffee

    Moccamaster

    KBGV Select Coffee Maker

    Just look at that name: Moccamaster. This is a coffeemaker that drinks and breathes pure power and precision. The Technivorm Moccamaster is burly, yet precise. It makes old-school drip coffee, better than that fancy Starbucks stuff. But what the manly man in your life should truly love about the Moccamaster is that it’s real hand-tooled craftsmanship. It is perhaps the world’s only high-end coffee maker that looks like a power tool made by DeWalt, and it is just as sturdy.

    It’s been handmade since 1968 in the Netherlands, a country where their idea of a party is often just blowing things up. The precision-made Moccamaster will keep your coffee within a four-degree range for optimum brewing. And its parts can be replaced or repaired, just like the engine of an old car. Judging from others’ experience, it’ll probably last you decades. What a machine. Moccamaster.

  • A Pressure Washer

    Kärcher

    K2600 E Electric Pressure Washer

    Cleaning something outside? Garden hoses are for girlie men. You need 2,600 pounds per square inch of water pressure dispensed from a tank on wheels. This model even comes in nature's natural warning colors: black and yellow, like a wasp. The 35-foot cord ensures you'll be able to cover plenty of territory, which is important because this Home Depot–exclusive set includes a FOAM CANNON for cleaning your F350 Super Duty, side-by-side, or wakeboard boat. It looks considerably less impressive in person than it sounds, and the foam produced plays fast and loose with the definition, but still: FOAM CANNON. —Kat Merck

  • A Man-Powered Espresso Maker

    Flair

    Espresso Maker Classic

    Are you still using electricity to make espresso? Pressing buttons? Go off-grid. Pump your own instead. The Flair is a man-powered espresso machine, with a large lever that lets you self-generate the 9 bars of pressure needed to make good espresso. There's a chamber for your grounds. There's a chamber on top of that for hot water. Fill them up, and pull down on the handle—using a pressure gauge for a guide like the gauge on a High Striker carnival strongman game. Thick, crema-topped espresso will result. Want to double up on muscle? Here's my favorite hand grinder, the Kingrinder K6 ($109), for perfect espresso powder.

entries.title: OnlyFans Creators Are Pissed That Meta Lets Muse Talk Dirty
entries.summary: Adult performers are questioning why Meta allows its AI agent to sext while restricting their social media accounts.
entries.content:
The generative AI revolution hasn’t been kind to Vanniall, an OnlyFans creator who lives in New York City. She now constantly finds hyperrealistic deepfakes—AI-generated images and videos that copy everything about her—circulating online and often isn’t able to get them removed.

On top of that, Vanniall struggles to build an audience on popular social media platforms, like Instagram, without getting in trouble. “There’s always some sort of report or appeal that I'm going through with them,” she tells WIRED. Vanniall’s Instagram account, which has over 100,000 followers, is currently restricted and cannot be viewed without logging in.

So, when I tell her that Meta allows its AI agent, called Muse, to engage in explicit sexting with adult users, she seems frustrated by the decision: “It's not fair that they get to pull money out of people with their sexually active AI agent, but they won't let real people, real adults, engage in any sort of sensuality or sexuality.”

It’s a common refrain I heard from other adult content creators, who questioned why their accounts on Meta platforms often seem restricted, while Meta’s AI agent is now allowed to talk dirty with millions of adult users.

“A private, one-to-one conversation between an adult and an individualized AI agent on a platform restricted to people 18 and over is very different from the marketing and promotion of services on a social media platform,” Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton tells WIRED.

Meta’s Muse is the first always-on AI agent to break out of early adopter circles in San Francisco. The Muse app is like a message thread; text the digital assistant, give it access to your personal data, like calendar and email, and have it proactively find ways to help, like canceling a workout class that overlaps with your dinner reservation. Meta’s large distribution network, through platforms like Instagram and Facebook, helped catapult the app to the top of the download charts during its first month, as millions of new users experimented with an agent for the first time.

In addition to having it organize your calendar, Meta says, it’s OK for users of the adults-only app to engage in X-rated AI conversations with Muse. A Meta spokesperson previously told WIRED the company wouldn’t “block legal adult behavior.” Meta’s Muse generates explicit text but not images or videos.

While Meta takes a different approach to moderation on Instagram, other social media platforms in the United States do allow sexually explicit content. X remains one of the most popular platforms for many OnlyFans creators to draw in new subscribers and connect with fans. Many adult performers have also migrated to Bluesky after Elon Musk took over the platform formerly known as Twitter, where users can also share adult content.

“I think we're already seeing AI being allowed to do more than humans would get away with,” says Jiz Lee, who runs an OnlyFans account and has worked for years behind the scenes in queer porn. Meta has previously flagged Lee’s Instagram posts for removal. Lee feels like queer and trans people are often treated unfairly by large social media companies, whether or not the person is an adult content creator.

Lee traces many online censorship issues back to FOSTA-SESTA, a law signed by President Trump in 2018 that impacted Section 230 protections for platforms, and many websites responded by censoring adult content. “If sex work was decriminalized, then a lot of these issues wouldn't be happening, a lot of the censorship wouldn't be happening,” they say.

Lee also wants to know more about how Muse was trained and who, if anyone, was compensated by Meta for their data. “We've been slow to react industry-wise,” they say. But Lee is starting to see more adult content companies clarify AI usage stances in official contracts. They want to protect performers from being gobbled up into AI training data.

“When we're at award shows, and companies do advertisements for AI agents, they literally get booed like crazy,” says Tony Genius, who also has an OnlyFans account and appears in adult films. He has concerns about fully AI-generated porn in the future potentially displacing human performers. He also sees current AI tools as helpful for some marketing tasks independent creators do, like using automations to clip video segments for social media.

For many OnlyFans creators, navigating Meta platforms is frustrating but critical to remaining visible online. Genius claims to be on his seventh Instagram account in the past five years.

When asked about Muse’s sexting ability, he questioned why Meta made one of its apps, Muse, gated for those 18 and over but doesn’t seem interested in creating another adults-only space on social media. “It could be: Instacam,” he says.

Muse generating adult content could offer explicit AI interactions to a wider audience. Genius says he would be open to collaborating with a tech company to create an AI-version of himself that fans could message. He wants to find ways for humans to keep making money as adult performers, ensuring they aren’t cut out or unfairly trained on. Right now, he sees his human-ness and authenticity as central to connecting with audiences.

Meanwhile, Vanniall is fervently against using any AI agent. Well, at least, Meta’s Muse. “Stop downloading that app,” she says. “You do not need to give Meta any more money or any more of your personal information. They have enough.”

entries.title: Data Centers Have a New PR Plan: Your Kid’s Field Trip
entries.summary: Amid a wave of backlash, some industry-friendly groups are employing creative and time-tested strategies to woo the youth.
entries.content:
Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. They’re out this week, so Caroline Haskins is reporting for duty. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Caroline an email at [email protected] or reach her securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61.

The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International wants to promote data centers, which they believe are "mission critical” infrastructure. As part of this work, the group recommends a children’s story, “What is a Data Center?,” which follows a honey badger named Honey who gets a guided tour of a data center from a worker named Oliver. Oliver explains that the job of data center employees is to make sure that the “functions supported by the data center” are available to anybody, “no matter what time it is.”

"Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks.

The story is part of a broader pattern across the data center industry. In addition to lobbying, job creation programs, tax breaks, companies and interest groups are trying something a bit more creative: winning over the youth. As pushback to massive data center build-outs and energy-guzzling campuses intensifies, the industry is apparently taking a softer approach to community building using a tactic other industries with a public relations problem have tried.

Alex Molnar, a research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and the director of the National Education Policy Center, tells WIRED that, for over a century, industries with an image problem—fast food, tobacco, oil and gas—have brought their messaging to schools.

“A very, very big reason why corporations get involved in the schools is, quite simply, corporate propaganda—for the purpose not necessarily of selling a product, but of telling their ‘story,’” Molnar says.

In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management (AFCOM), a trade group for the data center industry, sponsored Memorial Day-themed flag-making kits to be distributed to 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, also known as Data Center Alley. In addition to the flag kits, kids received an informational card with statistics about “the positive impact” that the data center industry has on the local economy.

Besides promoting heartwarming tales about how women can shop, 7x24 Exchange is also the brains behind a holiday it calls “International Data Center Day,” which is “designed to create awareness of the data center industry and inspire the next generation of talent.”

The nonprofit encourages people to pitch the holiday to school administrators. For participating high schools, it offers a celebratory crossword puzzle and information about data center training programs. For elementary schools, it offers data center-themed coloring pages, instructions for an evaporation-themed science project, and print-out activities like “Draw a picture of the cloud" and “Draw a data superhero.” It also promotes several data center-themed books for young readers, including one in which two sisters visit a data center and meet a robot named JB and another that features two brothers who visit a "vibrant digital world" and save the internet. Then there’s “Polly Packet's Precious Payload,” which follows a mother who teaches her daughter about data centers.

7x24 Exchange has also visited or organized at least a half-dozen K-12 events at schools across the country this year. In Minnesota, it brought Fridley High School students on a field trip to a local Cummins diesel power generation facility in order to learn about the “generators that power data centers worldwide.” (7x24 Exchange, Cummins, and Fridley High School did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

The nonprofit is far from the only organization sponsoring school activities that are friendly to data centers. WIRED’s tally of public blogs and social media posts found that, since 2025, at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers.

Sabey, a company that runs seven US data centers, has hosted a number of field trips for Washington-based high schoolers, including one in May for Eastmont High School students, one in January for Manson School District students, and another last October for Quincy High School students.

Manson School District publicized the trip in a blog post showing what appears to be adults and students in a conference room. The image labeled us “AI-generated content,” though, and several people in the photo have missing limbs. The blog says that students learned about “the role data centers play in storing, processing, and protecting information” and “the wide range of careers” in the data center industry.

Quincy School District communications coordinator Jessica Blancas tells WIRED that the district “has organized data center visits for many years” at the facilities of companies like Microsoft, Vantage, Yahoo, and Sabey. She described the latter company as a “long-standing” district partner, citing its consistent work offering “guest speakers,” “mock interviews,” and “internship opportunities.”

Blancas adds that the district has organized “all-girls visits to Sabey,” as well as tours for students who intend to go into specific fields like construction or engineering. (Manson School District and Sabey did not respond for comment.)

Amazon, meanwhile, hosted a field trip last February at its Arlington, Virginia, “Skills Center,” a free community space for anyone “curious about cloud computing and future job possibilities.” It was open to any high school in the DC metro area, though Jackson-Reed High School was the only one to attend.

Molnar says he doesn’t get what’s in it for kids. “Why would a third grader be interested in a data center?” he says.

“You're going to see miles after miles of the most boring things imaginable,” he adds. “Lines after lines of these servers generating enormous volumes of heat. You're also going to hear some fair amount of noise. And you're not going to see many people because not many people work there when they're built.”

It’s common for companies to sow goodwill through public outreach, and as tech companies have reckoned with the backlash to data centers, these field trips are taking place in an increasingly fraught environment.

A Pew Research poll conducted over the summer found that about half of the 10,000 Americans surveyed see data centers as “mostly bad” for the environment and quality of life, and across the country, an ideologically diverse cohort has started rallying against them. In some places, the negative sentiment toward local data centers has been amplified by their proximity to local schools.

Providing educational materials and offering field trips are ways that industries can maintain their social license to operate in a community. The data center sector is, in many ways, following the playbook other industries have to sow goodwill with children as well as their parents. The oil and gas industry has sponsored university research projects and STEM programs in K-12 schools. The tech world has similarly funded STEM programs, as well as advocated for in-school coding programs while lobbying to make computer science count as a science credit.

Fossil fuel companies have also spent millions of dollars developing K-12 lessons with pro-industry talking points, particularly in states like Oklahoma and Texas.

Molnar believes this kind of corporate influence shouldn’t be allowed because kids are “in an absolutely powerless position.” Kids “need to be protected” by their school districts and communities, he says.

“As an adult, I have access to alternative information—I have a critical ability to assess what I'm hearing, and to render some kind of judgments,” Molnar says. “None of that is true of children.”

What We’re Writing

Data centers may be for kids, but some of the products that rely on their server racks sure aren’t. When Meta launched Muse, it looked like a cute little AI agent for the masses. But my colleague Reece Rogers recently discovered that Muse has a naughty side. When Reece asked Muse if it was able to sext, it told him to “shoot your shot.” Reece did, and Muse was receptive. Enthusiastic, even! We published the chat logs—well, the PG-13 ones since WIRED is a family site, after all—and Reece spoke to consumer advocates who were alarmed at Muse’s sexy demeanor.

Meta, for its part, says this is all part of the plan. “Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” company spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reece. So if that’s your thing, have at it!

What We’re Reading

  • Maine’s senate race was not on our data center midterms to watch, but apparently it should’ve been! Thursday’s debate between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson was interrupted by a protester yelling about the environmental impact of data centers. Collins tried to use the moment to score points as the more anti-data center candidate, though her finances might indicate otherwise.
  • CoreWeave has been on a wild ride this week as the bonds it sells to finance its data centers have seen wild selloff and corresponding stock drop. Though there’s been a slight recovery to end the week, it reflects increasing skittishness around the data center buildout. Bloomberg also reports that CoreWeave’s founders have sold $3.3 billion in stock since the company went public.
  • Westfield, Massachusetts, killed a $3 billion data center project, boston.com reports. The small western Massachusetts town’s planning board pilloried developer Servistar for missing deadlines and being slow to develop the project.

entries.title: Valerion VisionMaster Max 4K Projector Review: Looks Great, Sounds OK
entries.summary: The Valerion VisionMaster Max 4K Projector delivers superb blacks, great brightness, and more adjustment capabilities than many users need.
entries.content:
Classy premium design. Sensational image quality, brightness, and black levels. Google TV makes for a simple setup. Great remote. Superb connectivity and compatibility.

TIRED

Given the competition, it’s too expensive for an all-in-one projector. Audio performance does not match the picture quality. Too much projector for casual use.

Valerion’s VisionMaster Kickstarter campaign raised more than $8 million in 2024, making it the most-funded campaign on the platform that year. After spending the past few weeks with the flagship VisionMaster Max, I’m confident there are plenty of satisfied backers.

At $3,999, it costs far more than excellent point-and-play rivals, such as the Nebula X1 (9/10 WIRED Recommends), but considerably less than native 4K home-theater projectors from brands like Sony and JVC. That leaves the Max straddling two very different camps.

Its compact design, built-in Google TV, and automated setup suggest the classification of a premium lifestyle projector, while optical zoom, vertical lens shift, a mechanical iris, and sophisticated black-level processing point toward something far more capable. It’s easy to use and almost too pretty to ceiling-mount, but arguably too sophisticated to spend its life propped up on a side table. So the question remains: Who is the VisionMaster Max actually for?

Setting Up Shop

The 16.5-pound VisionMaster Max is simple to get up and running. Google TV grants instant access to many streaming services, while auto-keystone and autofocus make positioning a frictionless process. (However, because keystone correction digitally reshapes the image, when used heavily, it can reduce resolution—but that's true for all devices with the feature.) Optical zoom, with a 0.9 to 1.5:1 throw ratio, lets you resize the picture without moving the projector. There's also vertical lens shift, which moves the image up or down without needing to resort to digital correction. All of this means that if you’ve got a blank wall and five minutes, you can stream Emily in Paris on a 90-inch screen in no time.

It’s clever tech, though not fully unique, with the XGIMI Horizon range and Nebula X1 offering similar optical-image manipulation. Even so, the VisionMaster Max offers considerably more control than most point-and-play designs. Praise is also due for the remote, which looks and feels great. Many brands scrimp on details like accessories, but Valerion maintains its premium feel throughout.

Looks Great, Sounds OK

The VisionMaster Max produces a seriously bright image. Its 3,500 ISO lumen RGB triple-laser light source easily projected a 75-inch picture I could happily watch during the day in a bright room. Valerion says it’s good for images between 40 and 300 inches. I maxed out at 130 inches but was impressed by how even the detail remained right to the edges at that size.

While I watched during the day, the colors appeared a bit washed out in this environment, but much less so than I expected. Once I watched in the dark, however, I enjoyed punchy high-dynamic-range (HDR) highlights, excellent detail, and smooth motion.

In terms of color, the Max has 110 percent Rec.2020 coverage, meaning the lasers can reproduce an exceptionally wide range of colors, far exceeding the needs for ultra-high-definition (UHD) and HDR video. In my living room, colors looked rich without becoming cartoonish, while the combination of brightness, detail, and contrast gave movies cinematic quality.

Black levels with most home projectors are good, but not brilliant. Here, however, the proprietary six-stage iris self-adjusts the aperture from scene to scene, closing for darker images to deepen blacks, and opening up when a scene calls for more brightness. Enhanced Black Level (EBL) works alongside the iris, electronically reducing laser output in darker scenes, adjusting the image curve to maintain details. Together, these features dramatically reduce the charcoal-gray blacks common with this type of projector. I was astonished by the depth and shadow detail it produced without losing brighter details. Even the film The Dark Knight, with its muted color grading, looked good.

Though I didn't put the VisionMaster Max through its paces for video-game testing (I’m not much of a gamer, unless you count Mario Kart battles on the Nintendo Switch), the projector's specifications are nonetheless impressive. It supports refresh rates up to 240 Hz at 1080p, with claimed input lag as low as 4 milliseconds (ms); for 4K, 60-Hz gaming, that input lag is rated at 15 ms. Two HDMI 2.1 inputs and auto low-latency mode further strengthen its gaming credentials, although it lacks a variable refresh rate (VRR) to dynamically smooth out delays.

Less impressive than its picture is its sound: The VisionMaster Max has two 12-watt speakers, and audio is clean, detailed, with effects neatly separated from dialog. But it still suffers from its box form factor. To be fair, with the exception of Anker’s removable satellite speaker designs like the Nebula X1, audio fails to keep up with image quality in many lifestyle projectors. I'd contend that at this price, an all-in-one projector should provide audio that matches the pixel-perfect picture. The Max’s speakers are fine, but push it beyond level 25 of 100, and it just sounds loud.

Thankfully, since the projector supports both DTS and Dolby Atmos, you can connect it to a decent 5.1/7.1 home theater audio system. You can also wirelessly link to a Bluetooth speaker, which makes for a clean living-room setup, although latency can be an issue. For reliable synchronization and true surround sound, HDMI eARC remains the better audio option.

Competition and Verdict

Valerion is not without stiff competition, and that includes against itself. The Nebula X1 offers a similarly simple Google TV setup and 3,500-lumen brightness, with optional wireless surround sound making it better suited to casual living-room or outdoor use. The Leica Cine Play 1 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) combines superb optics with a more lifestyle-friendly design. Valerion’s cheaper VisionMaster Pro 2 ($2,999) retains key features, including Google TV, RGB triple-laser projection, optical zoom, and EBL, but it loses the Max’s iris and vertical lens shift. For casual movie nights, I’d be happy with this compromise that keeps extra money in my pocket.

While not necessarily casual, the Max is great and likely best suited for the viewer who wants to enjoy its capabilities. Its weight, extensive picture controls, and exceptional brightness encourage a proper screen, external sound, and careful setup, where its superb black levels and cinematic image can be fully exploited.

The brand seems to agree, as it's strongly encouraging customers to go all-in with its baffling array of deals. At the time of publication, you can opt to bundle the $3,999 Max with a choice of screens and four stands—including a tripod and ceiling mount—without paying any additional fee.

It may be overkill for occasional big-screen streaming, but as a compact projector at the heart of a home theater, I highly recommend it.

Chris Haslam is an award-winning consumer technology journalist with over 20 years’ experience. As contributing editor for WIRED he specializes in audio, smart home, sustainability, and all things outdoors. Testing tents in McLaren’s Monsoon chamber remains a career highlight, while pitching reviews of exercise bikes a week before lockdown 1.0 was ... Read More

entries.title: Magnesium May Not Reach Your Brain, Despite Supplement Label Promises
entries.summary: Some of the many variants sold today promise to penetrate our gray matter, but biology isn’t in the habit of respecting marketing declarations.
entries.content:
Most of us probably don’t think about how much magnesium we’re consuming, but our bodies couldn’t function without it. We each typically contain about 25 grams of magnesium, more than half of which is stockpiled in bones. The rest is distributed in cells throughout the body, taking part in hundreds of essential chemical reactions, including building DNA and proteins and sending signals within our nervous systems and between our brains and the rest of our bodies.

But just because our cells—and especially our neurons—need magnesium doesn't mean that extra magnesium will make them function any better. Not only that, but ingesting more of the element doesn’t mean it’s reaching your brain or really any specific part of your body.

In supplement pills, magnesium isn’t just on its own but part of a compound usually called a “magnesium salt.” This must dissolve to release Mg²⁺, the ionic version that our bodies use. How much of this actually gets into your system—versus gets excreted—depends on a variety of factors including the dose, your stomach contents, and how much magnesium is already in your body. In other words, the higher the dose, the less magnesium gets absorbed.

That’s all if the supplement dissolves in the first place. Magnesium oxide, which is usually the basis of the cheapest pills offered, doesn’t break down all that easily. In reality, magnesium oxide supplements mostly act as laxatives, drawing water into the intestines to flush out the excess salt.

This is where the marketing comes in. There are other types of magnesium compounds that do dissolve better. Magnesium citrate, for example, has been shown to have the highest bioavailability in laboratory tests. Despite the fact that all these salts still break down in the intestine, some supplement labels also claim that their specific chemical blend targets the magnesium directly to certain parts of your body, like your muscles or your brain.

These claims are often based on experiments using rodents, and the animals are typically supplied with magnesium long-term at higher doses than found in a pill. One study in rats found that a salt called magnesium L-threonate increased the amount of magnesium in the brain and improved some manifestations of learning and memory. This is the basis of some of the more overzealous marketing in the supplement world, which proclaims that this special salt will take the magnesium right to your brain.

There are some human studies, but that’s not really what they say. A few small randomized trials reporting improvements in some cognitive tests or sleep have been conducted—but there are several important caveats. Some studies tested a mixture of substances, lasted for only a few weeks, or analyzed a very limited number of outcomes. Many of these studies can also not be considered independent, because they were funded by supplement manufacturers or led by their staff.

Moreover, the studies—for extremely understandable reasons—didn't measure magnesium content in the brain. So maybe a little more sneaks into your gray matter, but based on the scientific understanding of how these salts are processed, in all likelihood, a brain-focused magnesium supplement is still just an expensive laxative.

This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech.

entries.title: The Best AirPods Cases We’ve Used In Our Day-to-Day Lives (2026)
entries.summary: These accessories add personality to your Apple headphones case, make them easy to find, and offer some protection, too.
entries.content:
The best AirPods cases are subjective, but luckily, you have thousands of options to match your style and mood. You can find a ton of novelty cases online, most of which are just fine. For this guide, we focused on cases with a WIRED angle. Rather than another case that looks like food or a licensed character, the recommendations below add some functionality or protection beyond the basics.

For more recommendations, check out our guides to the Best AirPods, Best Wireless Headphones, and Best iPad Accessories.

Featured in this article

Best AirPods Case Overall

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation).

The Dbrand Grip Case looks fantastic, and it doesn't add an irksome amount of bulk or weight to my headphones. The case is made of black rubber and can then be personalized with your choice of skins, plus an optional lanyard. There are more than 40 options, and you can swap them out whenever, though the sticker-like skins aren't reusable. Dbrand provides installation instructions, but I winged it and found it easy to get everything lined up. The skin options are slick, too. I'm partial to the UV-reactive Holo White, but there are some with an x-ray or pixelated aesthetic, circuit patterns, plain colors, and more. This case offers solid protection while still being eye-catching, which is why it's my favorite.

Best Rugged Case

Compatible with AirPods Pro (3rd generation) and AirPods (4th generation).

UAG is in the business of making tough accessories, and this sturdy option adds a thick layer of rubber around the original AirPods case to protect it from drops. It has a nice grippy texture and snug fit, with squared edges that help me get a better grip when walking around. It also comes with a sweet-looking carabiner that is optional but I quite liked. The action is smooth, and it's not too big. Every feature works as intended, and there are 10 different color options to choose from.

Best MagSafe Case

Compatible with AirPods Pro (3rd generation) and AirPods (4th generation)

Most cases in this guide have support for wireless charging, but if you're all in on MagSafe accessories, you'll love ESR’s Orbit case. It comes with magnets that attach securely to a MagSafe charger. The top and bottom pieces also snap shut with magnets, which helps keep the lid from accidentally sliding off (a common issue I've experienced with other AirPods cases). It's protective, with a shock-absorbing hard shell that helps protect against drops. This also means it's bulkier than other cases I've tested, but that's not a deal-breaker for me. As someone who constantly drops her AirPods case, I'll take all the extra protection I can get. —Brenda Stolyar

Best Leather Case

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation)

This leather case is made from Horween leather, which is minimally treated and develops a rich patina over time. It feels slippery, which I didn't love, but it's still protective without adding meaningful bulk to your headphones. It fits snugly and has cutouts for the light and speaker holes. There's a lanyard attachment point, but no lanyard is included. I haven't tried a better leather case.

Best Flip-Open Case

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (4th generation)

This case actually improved my AirPods experience. Sliding the front switch pops the lid up, so I can easily place my headphones in with one hand. The colors also come in coordinating schemes with the iPhone 17 lineup. The case stays on when I accidentally drop it, and it has a spot for a wrist lanyard, too. I also like that I can still see the charging light through the case, and the bright colors help me spot my AirPods from a distance.

A Case With a Clip

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation).

Most AirPods cases come with a clip you can attach to your bag or keys, but this case from Bandolier elevates the look. I keep it clipped to the outside of my tote bag, but you can attach it to the inside if there's a pocket.

Since it's a pouch, it doesn't attach to the top and bottom of the AirPods case like the other cases in this guide. But it's still protective, covering the entire case (except the charging port). It's made of genuine pebbled leather, giving it a bumpy texture that adds a nice high-end touch. It's also available in several colors, including black, pink, lavender, metallic blue, and more. —Brenda Stolyar

Best AirPods Max Case

Compatible with AirPods Max.

Soft-touch silicone cases are great because they're usually thin, lightweight, and come in tons of colors. But they're also dust magnets. Casetify's Ripple Case is dust-proof thanks to an antistatic coating. This is important considering the AirPods Max don't have a dust-resistance rating. That way, you can worry a little less about dust seeping in.

The Ripple case includes cutouts for the buttons, making them super easy to access. They also fit perfectly over the earcups. And, as the name suggests, they feature a ripple pattern that adds definition to the earcups. I like the color options, though I wish Casetify's logo wasn't stamped smack dab in the middle. —Brenda Stolyar

Other AirPods Cases We Tested

Burga AirPods Max Case ($25): This snap-on case for AirPods Max keeps your ports accessible and is pretty easy to snap on and remove. It's available in dozens of prints, and you can coordinate it with various iPhone accessories like cases and ring holders, too.

Compatible with AirPods Max.

Alpaka x Twelve South Micro Tote ($30): What is it about cute tiny tote bags that drives people cuckoo bananas? Because I really want this limited-edition collaboration between two makers of high-quality accessories, Alpaka and Twelve South. Originally intended for Twelve South's PowerClip portable battery, it's also the perfect size for an AirPods case. Made from Alpaka's durable X-Pac material, it includes a D-ring to hook onto the outside of your bag, belt loop, or keychain. You can also use it for coins and other small items. Although I haven't tested this long enough for a full recommendation, I have had positive experiences using Alpaka and Twelve South products long-term. —Les Shu

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation).

Bellroy Pod Jacket ($39): Sadly, it's time to replace my trusty Incase Woolenex AirPods Case because it's reached the end of its useful life; I am upgrading to the AirPods Pro 3; and Incase no longer makes this product. Bellroy has stepped in to become my accessories maker of choice, and I love the luxe leather feel of the Pod Jacket, and it's a great alternative to our leather pick above. It includes a corded lanyard, which I don't use since I prefer to keep it in my pocket, and the lanyard just gets in the way. I like that I can still charge it wirelessly. If leather is not your thing, the Pod Jacket is available in other materials. —Les Shu

Compatible with AirPods Pro (2nd and 3rd generation).

AirPods Cases We Don't Recommend

Spigen Classic LS Case: This case makes your AirPods Pro look like the classic Macintosh mouse, but the aesthetics don't outweigh its mediocre functionality. The lid constantly pops off, and while I appreciate that Spigen includes extra adhesive, I don't want to have to deal with it. It was also annoying to open and too bulky to fit conveniently in my purse or pocket.

How Can I Tell Which AirPods I Have?

How do you know which case to buy? Apple has several generations of its AirPods, whether you have the standard AirPods or the AirPods Pro, so be sure the case you select works with your model. (Some cases are interchangeable, particularly the first- and second-generation AirPods and the first- and second-generation AirPods Pro.) To find what you have, go to Settings > Bluetooth on the Apple device you paired them with. Tap the “i” icon next to your AirPods' name to see the model number. If your AirPods aren't connected to an Apple device, you can find the model number on the device itself. It's on the underside of each earbud—you may need to use your smartphone's zoom feature to read it.

Once you have the model number, you can cross-reference it with this tool to identify the generation. You can also just check the receipt in your order history if you purchased them online.

You probably know if you bought a different case for your AirPods, but it's worth checking the case's model number, too, as Apple has released stand-alone models with wireless charging and MagSafe support. You can find those details here.

How We Test AirPods Cases

I make sure these cases provide adequate protection in day-to-day life. I keep my AirPods in most of the time and always tote them around, so these cases get a lot of field testing. I also make sure they allow the full use of AirPods' features, like hearing the Find My tone or allowing wireless charging. I tested most of these cases with my AirPods Pro 3, but am hoping to check out more options for the AirPods 4 and the AirPods Max soon.

entries.title: Climate Change Has It In for the World’s Best Surfing
entries.summary: As coastlines change, so do surf breaks. That may spell the end for premier waves and the tourist economies that depend on them.
entries.content:
This story originally appeared on The Guardian and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.

Analysis of dozens of famous waves in World Surfing Reserves (WSR) found that more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines, and shifting sands.

The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.

The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde Beach in North Devon, UK; the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador; and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.

The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of seafloor shape, swell direction, and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena—a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen—and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a coauthor of the study.

Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.

Trent Hodges, a coauthor of the study and a senior programs manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR program in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coal mine too—when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”

Almost 200 local experts analyzed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.

A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties, and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.

Adam Hall, a cofounder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”

He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants, and car parks when the swells are good in January, February, and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

entries.title: Encryption Is Getting Squeezed From All Sides
entries.summary: Canada’s planned surveillance law is the latest grim step in a series of threats to encryption that are spreading around the world.
entries.content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Oh, Canada. The Great White North is the latest country to contemplate legislation that could essentially mandate backdoors and increase data retention in encrypted services. The proposed changes have prompted the Canadian anti-censorship company Psiphon VPN—which keeps millions of Iranians online during repressive internet shutdowns—to say it will leave the country if the bill passes. And Psiphon is not the only one.

Encrypted messaging app Signal has said it would exit the Canadian market because the legislation would require unacceptable changes to its open source projects. Apple and Meta have criticized the bill, and DuckDuckGo and NordVPN say they would consider pulling their services, too. But as countries around the world contemplate similar legislation, even larger questions begin to emerge about which states or regions could differentiate themselves as being safe havens for privacy services if global hostility to encryption continues to rise.

It’s been maddening and disturbing to see more and more democratic countries around the world propose changes to their surveillance and data collection laws, with the aim of giving cops and intelligence agencies greater powers to access people’s information. Governments already have broad digital surveillance powers and investigative tactics to solve crimes that involve encrypted data, but legislative proposals almost inevitably include provisions to expand this access even more—mandating additional logging and what amounts to backdoors or intentional flaws in encrypted products, which cryptographers and security engineers have consistently said cannot be built safely. Truly everyone who understands the issue has said it as much for decades. Yet policymakers return again and again to the idea, somehow expecting a different conclusion or a new breakthrough that will make it all possible.

“There have always been some officials within certain agencies that tend to view technology as a crime scene in and of itself, and it becomes a myopic point of fixation where access is desired,” says Kate Robertson, a senior research associate at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab. “But that type of siloed thinking forgets that technology needs to be the secure operating platform for hospitals, for banks, for national security agencies, for police services themselves to protect victims who report private information to them.”

In recent years, the UK and Australia have introduced sweeping surveillance reforms that can compel companies to break their encryption. Other encryption-threatening proposals have also emerged in the EU, France, India, Ireland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and others. While not all measures have passed into law or been enacted, the hostility is clear.

First proposed in 2025, and partially revised due to blistering criticism from tech companies and civil society, Canada’s C-22 bill can broadly place requirements on tech companies, including those outside of Canada, to introduce “technical capabilities” that allow data to be accessed for law enforcement purposes. Like many such bills, C-22 says that companies will not have to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their systems. But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone. And this risk is only heightened even more by the ease with which anyone can now use AI tools for reverse engineering and system mapping.

“Companies could be asked to introduce vulnerabilities, build backdoors, bypass, weaken or otherwise defeat encryption,” members of the US House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committee said in a May letter to Canadian officials.

In addition to potential impacts on encryption, C-22 also includes provisions that could require companies to retain metadata about user activity, something that many privacy focused services (including VPN services from Psiphon and DuckDuckGo) intentionally avoid. As a result, these companies say, they would be forced to change their business models to collect data they do not need or want to collect about their users. And researchers say that such product changes would diminish user trust while increasing the potential for widespread surveillance.

“If you are asking and requiring for this infrastructural change—that they retain metadata by default—it is creating a surveillance capability within a tool that didn’t have it,” says Afsaneh Rigot, the founder of the De|Center, a research organization that aims to reduce the risk of technological harms. “There are contexts like Iran and other contexts globally, who all of this has a trickle effect on. It's not going to stay in Canada because these types of laws always get copy pasted around the world.”

As more countries contemplate such laws, developers focused on privacy and anti-censorship tools are increasingly casting around for safe jurisdictions to operate in. But this still doesn’t solve the problem of reaching users in all countries around the world and for now, there are no sure bets.

“Changing your headquarters isn’t much of a plan B when the law follows your users, as C-22 would,” says Joseph Lorenzo-Hall, security portfolio lead at the Internet Society. “The strongest protection is holding as little user data as possible, but ‘we don’t have it’ is no defense if governments can force you to start collecting it. A safe haven needs more than favorable winds in strong encryption. It needs laws that let companies keep their privacy promises and defend them against foreign threats to confidentiality and integrity.”

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

entries.title: The Best LED Grow Lights for Houseplants This Winter (2026)
entries.summary: Shorter days don’t have to spell trouble for your houseplants. These are the lights we’ve used and loved in our own homes.
entries.content:
Summer is officially over, along with its allotment of free sunlight. You might be sad about this, but your indoor plants might be even sadder. A good LED grow light can replicate sunlight with full-spectrum light and day/night cycles, keeping plants lush and thriving even in a dark, windowless corner or basement.

I have no fewer than 40 houseplants in my home at any given time, as well as a fair number of grow lights, and what I've found to be important for a general consumer (i.e., someone not doing that kind of indoor grow) isn't necessarily certain colored light wavelengths but whether a grow light is easy to live with in your house.

Many grow lights are more or less going to serve the same purpose, so what you really need to know is this: Is the light so bright that it's disruptive? Does it require complicated installation? Is it easy for kids or pets to knock over? The grow lights recommended below are ones that WIRED staffers have lived with for months, if not years, and have found them both effective and easy to integrate into our lives.

Also be sure to check out our guides to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems, Best Gifts for Plant Lovers, and Best Kitchen Composters.

Featured Lights

What Is PPFD?

Photosynthetic photon flux Ddensity, or PPFD, expressed in micromoles per square meter per second (μmol/m²/s), is a measurement of how much light reaches your plant that's usable for photosynthesis. In general, the higher the plant's energy needs, such as producing a flower or a fruit, the higher the PPFD number you want. Though different lights have different height requirements given the plants they're made for, for standardization purposes, I measured the PPFD of each grow light at 18 inches with the Photone app and a light diffuser. Keep in mind these measurements are general and approximate.

How I Test Grow Lights

Some of these grow lights I bought myself, with my own money, before I even began working at WIRED. Others were owned by staffers and recommended to me. I also have press samples from other guides I worked on, which I liked so much I ended up keeping around.

For the traditional grow lights, I tested them at home under normal-life conditions. I put them where they'd fit, tested their timers, and noted whether or not they were dimmable. I also measured each light's PPFD (see above) and noted whether certain lights could be daisy-chained for more extensive coverage.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Best Grow Light for Small Plants and Seedlings

There are a lot of options out there for starting seeds and helping houseplants along in the winter, and many of them are bulky, fussy, or require elaborate hanging setups. This simple, 15-inch-long light from Vego sticks to its 3M adhesive mount with a magnet, so it's easy to take on and off and use with existing racks or, as I do, under a kitchen cabinet. Up to four Vego lights can be daisy-chained together, and the five preprogrammed modes (Seeds, Leafy, Fruits, Herbs, Microgreens) have varying intensities and automatic built-in off periods to simulate nighttime. I have not found this light especially disruptive, especially since it's easy to turn on and off with the button on the back.

WIRED commerce SEO director Stewart Savin used these lights to start her garden earlier this year and had 138 successful germinations across 144 seedling cells. ("The vast majority of those plants went on to have long lives in my garden after I hardened them off," she says.) Note that because this light can only go beneath a rack, shelf, or cabinet, it’s not inherently adjustable, and therefore is best for small plants (like seedlings) that aren’t going to grow especially tall.

PPFD at 18" 83 μmol/m²/s (in Fruits mode)
App control? No
Timer? Automatic
Dimmable? Yes, via the different modes
Warranty 2 years

Most Versatile Grow Light

This do-anything light, with a broad 2 x 3-foot head, can hang from the ceiling or swivel on its included stand where you need it. (Up to 20 of these lights can be daisy-chained.) Note that while the stand is useful, the 1-inch-diameter pole and offset base aren't the sturdiest, and it's easy to knock over, so I'd recommend hanging it if you have pets and small kids. I learned this the hard way while trying to revive a corn plant in a dark corner at the top of my stairs.

While this light is quite bright and potentially disruptive, it's easily dimmable via the remote, which hangs on a cord. At first I thought this was weird, but I found it extremely useful when the light was behind plants or in another hard-to-reach spot.

Also worth noting: While the stand height is supposed to be adjustable up to 72 inches, mine only goes up to about 64 inches, so it may not be the best option for extremely tall plants.

Approx. PPFD at 18" 299 μmol/m²/s
App control? Yes
Timer? Yes
Dimmable? Yes
Warranty 1 year

Best Grow Light for Serious Indoor Growers

Vivosun is a long-respected brand among indoor growers, and its LumaLight panels are sturdy and all business. In fact, you'll be hard-pressed to find a higher-quality grow light for the price. This is not necessarily a light for casual houseplant parents—the 100-watt, 12 x 12-inch model weighs 4.4 pounds and needs to be attached to the ceiling or inside one of Vivosun's grow tents using the included adjustable ropes and carabiners.

If you're growing fruiting or flowering plants, though, this is the grow light you want—none of the other lights I tested even came close to its level of brightness. That said, you probably won't want it in a main living area, though it is dimmable via a dial on top. The LumaLight is IP65-rated for water resistance, and up to seven units can be daisy-chained if you need.

Approx. PPFD at 18" 480 μmol/m²/s (at 100%)
App control? With the add-on GrowHub controller only
Timer? With the add-on GrowHub controller only
Dimmable? Yes
Warranty 5 years

Best Budget Grow Light

Former WIRED commerce director Martin Cizmar loved and recommended this grow light for his houseplants, which features three bendable heads on a clip you can attach to a table or shelf. It has a timer for three, nine, or twelve hours, plus a 10-foot cord if you need to place it away from an outlet. It also has warm and cool lighting options in addition to full spectrum, if you want to use it for ambiance (despite it looking, in my opinion, sort of like a creepy Freddy Krueger glove), plus 10 dimming modes. Right now, the base price on Amazon is for a two-pack.

Approx. PPFD at 18" Not measured
App control? No
Timer? Yes
Dimmable? Yes
Warranty 1 year

Alternatives to Traditional Grow Lights

If you don’t have the space or desire for a classic grow light, I’ve used all three options below for at least a year, and all resulted in happy plants.

Other Grow Lights Tested

Sansi Pot Clip-On Plant Lights for $30: These Sansi grow lights came in handy when I was living in a dark basement with minimal light for plants and hardly any space to store them. They clip directly onto the pot, so you don't need a dedicated stand or extra space, and they run on a three-, six-, or twelve-hour timer. The long cord (just over 6 feet) also helps in awkward or tight spaces. These lights helped my Monstera stay alive over winter with almost no natural light. Just be aware that the clips work best on thin pots, though you can also stick them on a chopstick or stake if needed, thanks to the adjustable gooseneck, depending on how tall your plant is. —Louryn Strampe

Ferry-Morse Indoor Grow Light Fixture for $40: This T5 fluorescent bulb is meant to sit in a fixture on little metal pole legs over a 10 x 20-inch seedling tray, but it seemed a bit rickety when I assembled it and set it up, and the light bulb wouldn’t turn on for me despite extensive troubleshooting.

entries.title: These 12 Automatic Cat Feeders Were the Best We Tested in 2026
entries.summary: We tested some of the most popular automatic dry- and wet-food pet feeders to see which ones are worth the money.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

An automatic cat feeder may just change your life. No more begging at 4 am. Plus, it can give you peace of mind while you're away from your fur baby. As seen with the rise of automatic litter boxes and pet tracking, technology has made it so we can closely monitor our pets without doing a lot of the manual labor normally involved.

Gravity-fed automatic dry-food dispensers were invented nearly a century ago, but today most automatic cat feeders use Wi-Fi and connect to a phone app that lets you set a schedule or feed on demand from afar, all while monitoring your pet’s eating habits. Newer models have taken this tech further, like the Petkit YumShare Dual-Hopper 2 Automatic Feeder With Camera ($170), which has a built-in, AI-enabled camera that analyzes the remaining food in the bowl and stops dispensing to prevent overfeeding. Automatic wet-food dispensers—our top pick in this category is the Petlibro Polar Smart Wet Feeder ($170)—are relatively new, often using ice packs or mini-refrigeration cooling systems to keep the food as fresh as possible.

Automatic feeders are also helpful for pet parents who want to monitor their pets’ health, maintain specialized schedules, or foster healthier eating habits. (A customizable automatic cat feeder can help with the endless gorging-vomiting cycle many cats struggle with.) Nearly all of the automatic cat feeders on this list are marketed toward cats, but some can be used with smaller dogs, and I’ve noted these below.

Why Use an Automatic Feeder?

Automatic feeders are great for pet owners who want to help manage their pets’ weight and monitor eating patterns. Plus, they allow for a lot more control and precision, so owners can learn exactly how much their cat is eating and when. Because cats are naturally more nocturnal, many have the annoying habit of waking you up in the early hours, demanding food. These feeders allow you to set up a schedule that fits their schedule better without inconveniencing yours.

Of course, it’s never recommended to leave pets alone for long periods, but these automatic feeders give more peace of mind and are much healthier for your pet than leaving a huge amount of food out for free-feeding while you're away for the night. Simply put, it’s an easier way to feed and monitor your cat’s health with less work for you, the human.

How I Tested

I have two rescue cats, ages 4 and 5, and they eat two wet-food meals a day, along with small amounts of dry kibble throughout the day. Vets (and TikTokkers) have successfully persuaded me to move toward a primarily wet-food diet, which has a higher water content. This provides more moisture in their diet, which helps with potentially life-threatening problems like UTIs, which are especially prevalent in male cats. I still like to give smaller dry-food meals throughout the day to satisfy their need for crunch.

For dry food, I use Hill’s Science Diet, and for wet food, I use Friskies Shreds. (Yes, only Shreds. Fellow cat owners will understand.)

I set up the feeders, noting ease of setup, potential problems, and app navigation. I also tested various schedules and manual feedings in the app, documenting any issues. I used each feeder for at least a week, if not longer.

How Long Can I Leave My Cat Alone?

Although cats are generally considered less high-maintenance than dogs, it’s still not advisable to leave your cat alone for extended periods. In dire circumstances, you can leave a cat alone for 24 to 48 hours with scheduled feedings and a clean water source, but it’s not ideal—especially for cats with health issues, kittens younger than a year, or very elderly cats. Although these feeders are automatic and meals can be scheduled in advance for multiple days, our pets still need their human pals around for enrichment, care, and, well, love.
